## Summary

`Tree.chomsky_normal_form()` binarizes a parse tree and defaults to right factoring. For a node with N children the right-factor branch repeatedly removes the first element of a working list with `list.pop(0)`, which shifts all remaining elements each time, so binarizing one wide node costs O(N^2). An application that converts an attacker-supplied treebank tree to Chomsky Normal Form can be forced into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU by one wide flat tree. No authentication or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

In the default right-factor branch the transform executes `curNode[0:] = [nodeCopy.pop(0), newNode]` inside a loop over the N children of a node. `list.pop(0)` is O(len) because it shifts every remaining element down by one; performed N-2 times over a shrinking length-N list this sums to O(N^2). The left-factor branch instead uses `nodeCopy.pop()` (removing the last element), which is O(1) and linear overall, so the two branches differ only by this front-versus-back removal. No cap is placed on the child count of a node, and the public `Tree.fromstring` parser accepts an arbitrarily wide bracketed tree.

```text
Affected function:
- nltk.tree.transforms.chomsky_normal_form (nltk/tree/transforms.py; right-factor sink at line 168, O(1) left control at line 179)
Public entry points: nltk.tree.Tree.chomsky_normal_form (nltk/tree/tree.py:455, default factor="right"); nltk.tree.Tree.fromstring (nltk/tree/tree.py:592).

An attacker who can influence the tree that an application normalizes to Chomsky Normal Form causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). Because the cost grows quadratically with the attacker-chosen child count, roughly 1.5 MB of treebank input costs about 14 seconds on one core and scales as N^2 above that. advisories.summary: NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in ConllCorpusReader SRL instance builder via nested span rescan

## Summary

`ConllCorpusReader.srl_instances()` builds semantic-role-labeling instances from a CoNLL corpus block. For a sentence block with P predicates and P span columns, the instance builder rescans every span column (and every span within it) once per predicate while searching for each predicate's head, giving O(P^2 * R) work. A single well-formed block that places the head span in the last column forces the full scan on every predicate, so an application that reads an attacker-supplied CoNLL SRL corpus can be driven into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU. No authentication or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

`_get_srl_instances` iterates over the P predicates of a block; for each predicate it scans every span list and every span within it, using an inner `break` that stops only when a span tagged `V` or `C-V` containing the predicate word is found. When the sole head span is placed in the last span column, no earlier column matches, so the `for ... else: continue` construct traverses every span of every earlier column before matching. Over P predicates each scanning up to P columns of R spans, the cost is O(P^2 * R). The block is read whole with no size cap, and the grid-consistency check enforces only uniform column count, not a bound on P, R, or total work.

```text
Affected function:
- nltk.corpus.reader.conll.ConllCorpusReader._get_srl_instances (nltk/corpus/reader/conll.py:394-424; nested rescan at lines 405-419)
Public entry point: nltk.corpus.reader.conll.ConllCorpusReader.srl_instances (nltk/corpus/reader/conll.py:158-169).
```

## Impact

An attacker who can supply a CoNLL corpus that an application loads and iterates with `srl_instances()` causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). The path is network-reachable through any corpus-ingestion surface (AV:N) and needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N, UI:N). ## Summary

`BllipParser` in `nltk/parse/bllip.py` hands caller-supplied filesystem paths to the native `bllipparser` C extension without routing them through NLTK's `pathsec` validation. Every sibling tool wrapper applies it. `BllipParser` applies none of it: the module imports only `ParserI`, `safe_print`, and `Tree`, with zero `pathsec` references, so the three model-path parameters reach the C extension unchecked. advisories.summary: ag-psd can exhaust memory when parsing crafted PSD dimensions
advisories.description:
### Summary
readPsd() commits the image/layer buffers from the declared header geometry (width x height x channels x depth, and per-layer rectangles) before validating those values against the actual data. A tiny crafted PSD declaring huge geometry forces a multi-gigabyte allocation.

### Impact
On ag-psd 30.2.0, Node 24, a 52-byte PSD makes readPsd(buf) commit ~3.17 GB (measured peak RSS) in ~0.45 s before throwing a catchable RangeError ("Offset is outside the bounds of the DataView") — about 61,000,000x amplification. Because the buffer is committed before validation, the allocation OOM-kills the process before the error on essentially any host (uncatchable), and concurrent requests exhaust memory. Any service reading untrusted PSDs with ag-psd is exposed to a remote DoS.

This is distinct from #39 and #206, which involve genuinely large PSDs (memory proportional to real data). Here the input is 52 bytes: the file declares enormous geometry that is never present, so the allocation is driven by an unvalidated header field, not by actual content, an uncontrolled-allocation denial-of-service vulnerability, not proportional memory use.

### Steps to reproduce
The PoC is a 52-byte PSD (sha256 a1146a6fabdfef289472f99a56851249e7a46e8d19d4d8bf85fe833e2f0158b6). Reconstruct with:

    base64 -d > poc.psd <<'EOF'
    OEJQUwABAAAAAAAAAA0AADcuAAA58wAgAAMAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAdEgNZv+i9bc9ygd2A==
    EOF

Then (commits ~3.17 GB before throwing a catchable RangeError):

    const { readPsd } = require('ag-psd');
    const buf = require('fs').readFileSync('poc.psd');
    readPsd(buf.buffer.slice(buf.byteOffset, buf.byteOffset + buf.byteLength));

### Root cause
psdReader.js sizes the off-heap typed-array buffers from the declared header dimensions (and per-layer rectangles, a second independent lever) before validating against the available bytes.

### Suggested fix
Validate the declared dimensions, channel count, depth, and per-layer rectangles against the actual input length (and a sane maximum) before allocating.

advisories.summary: File Browser: Trailing-slash directory deletion leaves public shares active for recreated paths
advisories.description:
## Summary

File Browser v2.63.15 can leave a public directory share behind when the shared directory is deleted through a path with a trailing slash. The share cleanup path calls `DeleteWithPathPrefix(file.Path, userID)`, but the Bolt backend performs the database prefix query with the unnormalized argument before trimming the slash for boundary checks. For a stored share at `/a`, deleting `/a/` queries for paths prefixed by `/a/`, so the exact `/a` share is never loaded and never deleted.

If a directory with the same path is later recreated, the stale public share becomes active again and exposes the new directory contents through the old public URL.

## Impact

advisories.summary: NLTK: Quadratic CPU exhaustion in LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize via unguarded onset reversal loop

## Summary

`LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize` in the NLTK tokenizer package contains an unguarded O(n^2) processing loop. When the method is called on a single token that consists of a long run of vowels (for example `"a" * n`), it consumes CPU time proportional to the square of the token length. An attacker who can supply an untrusted token to this public tokenizer API can force a single request to saturate one CPU core for a prolonged period, degrading availability of any service that syllabifies attacker-controlled text. No authentication, special configuration, or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

The method walks the token in reverse and, on every iteration after the first vowel is seen, evaluates the membership test `char_lower + current_onset[::-1] in self.legal_onsets`. The set `legal_onsets` is built by `onset()`, which returns only the characters up to the first vowel, so every member is vowel-free. For an all-vowel token the first branch can therefore never match, `onset` never becomes `True`, and the reset branch that would clear `current_onset` is never reached. As a result `current_onset` grows by one character on every iteration. Building `current_onset[::-1]` and hashing the resulting string costs O(k) on iteration k, and this is repeated for k from 1 to n, giving total cost O(n^2). The security invariant that is violated is bounded per-token work: there is no length cap on this code path, so untrusted token length translates directly into quadratic CPU consumption.

Source: nltk/tokenize/legality_principle.py (membership-test sink at line 133; loop over token[::-1] beginning at line 126)
Helper establishing the vowel-free onset set: LegalitySyllableTokenizer.onset (nltk/tokenize/legality_principle.py, returns prefix up to first vowel)
```

An attacker who controls a token passed to `LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize` can trigger quadratic CPU work. In the reviewed release a token of roughly 64,000 vowel characters takes about 1.8 seconds on a single core, and the cost grows with the square of the length, so a token in the hundreds of kilobytes to megabyte range consumes a core for many seconds to minutes. Memory use is linear. advisories.summary: NLTK: Unbounded CPU consumption in SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.parse() with ambiguous or self-embedding grammars
advisories.description:
## Summary

`nltk.parse.recursivedescent.SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.parse()` performs an unbounded top-down search over ambiguous or self-embedding context-free grammars with no wall-clock or step limit. An actor who can influence the grammar and supply a short input to a caller that uses this parser can force a single `parse()` call to pin a CPU core indefinitely, producing a denial of service. The related base class `RecursiveDescentParser` gained a `max_time` wall-clock deadline, but the stepping subclass drives its own step loop and never arms or consults that deadline, and its constructor does not accept a `max_time` parameter, so the guard cannot be enabled on this path.

## Root Cause

`RecursiveDescentParser` bounds its recursive search inside `_parse`: it arms a wall-clock deadline on the first step and raises `TimeoutError` once `max_time` (default 5.0 seconds) is exceeded. `SteppingRecursiveDescentParser` was designed for interactive single-stepping and overrides both `parse()` and `_parse`. Its `parse()` runs `initialize()` followed by a `while self.step() is not None` loop that never enters the guarded base `_parse`. Its `_parse` override is a state-capturing stub that records history and returns a sentinel, and it never references the inherited `self._parse_deadline` or `self._max_time`. Its `__init__` signature omits `max_time` entirely, so a caller cannot enable or tighten a bound. The security invariant that a single parse must terminate within a bounded time is therefore never enforced on this parser.

```text
Affected component: nltk.parse.recursivedescent.SteppingRecursiveDescentParser
- parse()      nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:428-433  (drives its own step loop, no bound armed or checked)
- _parse()     nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:643-668  (stub override; never consults self._parse_deadline / self._max_time)
- __init__()   nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:410-418  (signature (self, grammar, trace=0); no max_time parameter)
Base guard for comparison: RecursiveDescentParser._parse nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:141-150
```

## Impact

An actor who controls or influences the grammar passed to `SteppingRecursiveDescentParser` and can supply a short token sequence to a caller that invokes `parse()` can cause that call to never return. The top-down search enumerates a derivation space that grows on the order of the Catalan numbers with no memoization of the search and no deadline, so one crafted grammar plus a short input determinist

advisories.summary: NLTK: Symlink escape in YCOECorpusReader lets a psd/pos directory symlink read files outside the corpus root within the data sandbox
advisories.description:
## Summary

`YCOECorpusReader` builds two nested corpus sub-readers whose roots are derived from `self.root.join("psd")` and `self.root.join("pos")` (nltk/corpus/reader/ycoe.py). Because `FileSystemPathPointer.join()` (nltk/data.py) performs a purely lexical containment check and never resolves symlinks, and because `CorpusReader.__init__` (nltk/corpus/reader/api.py) validates a sub-reader root only against the global NLTK data sandbox and not against the enclosing corpus root, a directory symlink named `psd` or `pos` planted inside a YCOE corpus lets the reader anchor its nested sub-readers outside the YCOE corpus root. An attacker who controls the contents of a YCOE corpus loaded under `pathsec.ENFORCE=True` can make `parsed_sents()`, `tagged_words()`, and related methods return file content from other locations inside the allowed data sandbox, defeating the per-corpus-root containment boundary the pathsec controls are meant to enforce.

## Root Cause

NLTK's pathsec controls are designed to keep each corpus reader confined to its own corpus root. The scoped containment is enforced through `validate_path(..., required_root=self._root)` at read time. However, the containment invariant is violated at reader-construction time for nested readers:

- `FileSystemPathPointer.join()` accepts a component that is a directory symlink because it only checks the joined string lexically (`os.path.normpath` plus a `startswith` prefix test) and never calls `resolve()`.
- `CorpusReader.__init__` validates the resulting sub-reader root string, but calls `validate_path` without `required_root`, so only the global-sandbox layer runs; the scoped per-corpus-root layer is skipped. The symlink is resolved by that global check, its target is found to be inside the allowed sandbox, and the sub-reader is accepted with its root pointing at the escaped target.

From that point every read the sub-reader performs is scoped to the already-escaped root, so no later guard re-anchors it to the YCOE corpus root.

```text
Affected functions:
- nltk.corpus.reader.ycoe.YCOECorpusReader.__init__   (nltk/corpus/reader/ycoe.py) builds nested sub-readers from self.root.join("psd")/("pos") without containing them to the parent root
- nltk.corpus.reader.api.CorpusReader.__init__        (nltk/corpus/reader/api.py) validates a sub-reader root only against the global sandbox (validate_path without required_root)
- nltk.data.FileSystemPathPointer.join               (nltk/data.py) applies a lexical pref

advisories.summary: dnspython has excessive memory and CPU use
advisories.description:
### Summary

A maliciously crafted zone file could use a WKS record to consume excessive memory and CPU, possibly causing the process to exit due to memory exhaustion.

### Details

The `from_text()` parser does not check that a WKS record service number is between 0 and 65535 inclusive.  It then uses this number to resize the bitmap to accommodate a bit with that offset.  This can cause extremely large memory allocations, and also extends the array very inefficiently, wasting CPU.

### Proof of concept

This demonstrates the failure to limit the service number, though with a value that does not cause excessive memory or CPU consumption.

```
rd = dns.rdata.from_text("IN", "WKS", "10.0.0.1 udp 65536")
```

### Impact

If dnspython is used to read zonefile format where the attacker can control the type and rdata text, the program may consume excessive memory or CPU, denying service.

advisories.summary: OpenTelemetry JavaScript: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File and Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor in @opentelemetry/instrumentation-http
advisories.description:
### Summary

`@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http` redacts sensitive URL query parameters on **outgoing (client) spans** but not on **incoming (server) spans**. The server-span path writes the raw query string verbatim into the `url.query` attribute, so credentials embedded in inbound request URLs — AWS presigned-URL signatures, Azure SAS tokens (`sig`), GCS signed-URL signatures — are exported in plaintext to the configured tracing backend.

Configuring the `redactedQueryParams` option **does not change this**, as this applies only to outgoing (client) spans.

### Impact

**Information disclosure / credential leakage** (CWE-200; CWE-532, insertion of sensitive information into telemetry data).

**Who is impacted:** any Node.js service instrumented with `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http` — directly or transitively via `@opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node` — that receives inbound requests carrying credentials in the query string. Common cases: services fronting presigned S3/GCS downloads, Azure SAS-token URLs, and signature-authenticated webhooks.

**Consequence:** clients' still-valid credentials are written into server spans and stored by the tracing backend, readable by anyone with span-read access — observability vendor infrastructure, dashboard users, and internal audiences far broader than the credential's intended scope. Presigned-URL signatures typically remain valid for minutes to days after capture, so this is not merely historical exposure.

**Severity:** Moderate. Exploitation requires read access to the telemetry backend, and inbound URLs must actually carry signed credentials. However, the gap is a documented mitigation that silently fails to apply, which defeats the mitigation operators would reach for.

### Patches

This vulnerability has been patched in `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http` version `0.222.0`.
Known sensitive query string values (as defined by Semantic Conventions) are redacted by default from span data for incoming spans.
The `redactedQueryParamsServer` configuration option was added for customization.

advisories.description:
## Summary

OpenTelemetry Go eagerly materializes W3C baggage metadata into property objects during parsing. Slice growth, serialization, and copying into the internal representation cause **bounded but disproportionate memory-allocation amplification** for a valid, densely populated header. In v1.46.0 and v1.47.0-rc.1, the 8,192-byte raw-input limit is checked before member parsing; this is not unlimited allocation or a bypass of that limit.

A valid 8,191-byte value containing one member and 4,094 properties causes approximately 778 KB of cumulative allocation per parse. A corrected measurement with forced garbage collection before and after parsing retains approximately 164 KB per result while it remains live. These are different metrics: approximately 95 times the input in allocation traffic versus approximately 20 times in incremental live heap in the measured environment.

The relevant security configuration is a service that enables Baggage propagation and extracts attacker-controlled inbound context before authentication or on a public route. Concurrent or sustained requests can increase allocation and GC pressure. The evidence establishes allocation amplification, but does not establish reliable OOM, process termination, or complete denial of service.

This is a **pre-existing, independent allocation-amplification path not addressed by GHSA-5wrp-cwcj-q835 / CVE-2026-41178**. It predates that advisory; it is not described as having been introduced by its fix.

## Affected module, versions, and symbols

- Go module: `go.opentelemetry.io/otel`.
- Import paths and entry points: `go.opentelemetry.io/otel/baggage.Parse` and `go.opentelemetry.io/otel/propagation.Baggage.Extract`.
- Implementation: `parseMember`, property-slice growth and serialization, and conversion into `internal/baggage.Item`.
- Source history places the eager-property implementation at commit `4bf6150fa94e18bdf01c96ed78ee6d1c76f8e308`, first included in `v1.0.0-RC1`; the stable release line starts at `v1.0.0`.

- Patched release: `v1.47.0` (https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go/pull/9024), which validates and normalizes W3C property metadata in place during `Parse` and materializes `Property` structs lazily only when `Member.Properties()` is explicitly called.

advisories.summary: sqlite3-ruby: Possible SQL query truncation when a string is 4 GiB or larger
advisories.description:
### Summary

sqlite3-ruby cast Ruby string lengths (`long`) to `int` before passing them to SQLite. On 64-bit platforms, a string of 4 GiB (2^32 bytes) or larger had its length wrap, so SQLite saw only the first `length mod 2^32` bytes. An attacker who controls the length of a SQL string could truncate the query, for example dropping a trailing `WHERE` clause. The affected paths are:

- the SQL passed to `Database#prepare`, `#execute`, and related methods
- String and Blob values passed to `Statement#bind_param` and related methods
- String and Blob values returned from SQL functions and aggregates defined in Ruby (`Database#create_function`, `#create_aggregate`, and related methods)

sqlite3 v2.10.2 raises `RangeError` when any of these strings is longer than `INT_MAX` bytes.

### Severity

The sqlite3-ruby maintainers have evaluated this as medium severity (CVSS 4.8). Exploitation requires an attacker to get at least 4 GiB into a single SQL string or bound value. Most deployments reject a request body that large before the application sees it, and the server must hold several copies of the string in memory.

A truncated bound value is only a prefix of the attacker's input, so the bind paths matter only where the application validated the full value. A truncated SQL string is more serious: when the attacker's input is inlined into the SQL, the clauses that follow it are dropped. If a dropped clause contained a bind placeholder, binding raises `SQLite3::RangeException` instead of running the query.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to sqlite3 v2.10.2 or later.

As a workaround for earlier versions, reject SQL strings and bound values of 4 GiB or larger before passing them to sqlite3-ruby, or limit request body size well below 4 GiB.

### Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by Luke Jahnke from elttam.

advisories.summary: AutoMapper: Denial of Service via uncontrolled recursion that bypasses MaxDepth
advisories.description:
### Summary
The default and explicit `MaxDepth` limits added for CVE-2026-32933 don't apply to several mapping paths. Mapping a deeply nested source through any of them recurses without bound and throws a `StackOverflowException`, which can't be caught and terminates the process.

### Affected paths
- **Polymorphic maps:** derived type maps (`Include` / `IncludeBase`) didn't inherit the base map's `MaxDepth`, and the default limit for self-referential maps was only applied to the base map. A chain of derived objects was mapped without a limit, even with `MaxDepth` set on the base map.
- **Runtime-typed members:** members typed as `object` or an interface aren't seen by self-reference detection, so the default limit isn't applied.
- **Dictionary and dynamic sources:** mapping a nested `Dictionary<string, object>` or `ExpandoObject` (for example, deserialized JSON) onto typed destinations recurses with no depth tracking. `MaxDepth` has no effect.
- **Recursive type converters:** `ConvertUsing` that calls `context.Mapper.Map` ignores `MaxDepth`.

### Impact
An application that maps attacker-influenced, deeply nested data through one of these paths can be crashed. On a 1 MB stack (the Windows default), a few thousand levels of nesting are enough.

### Fix
- Derived type maps inherit `MaxDepth`, and the default limit is applied to them.
- Every runtime map call checks for sufficient stack, and fails with a catchable `InsufficientExecutionStackException` instead of overflowing.

### Workarounds
Set `MaxDepth` explicitly on derived maps and on maps reached through `object` or interface members. There is no configuration workaround for dictionary or dynamic sources, or for recursive type converters, other than limiting input depth before mapping.

### Related
- CVE-2026-32933 (GHSA-rvv3-g6hj-g44x)
- GHSA-6vhm-j9h7-f9gh: `MaxDepth` not enforced through constructor parameters and positional records, fixed in the same releases.

advisories.summary: Astro: XSS via attribute injection in dynamic tag names
advisories.description: ## Summary When a dynamic tag (`const Tag = ...; `) resolves to a string, Astro renders it as a raw HTML element name. The name was filtered to remove characters that could inject attributes, but the filter did not handle `/`. Because HTML parsers treat `/` inside a tag as an attribute separator, a tag name such as `img/src/onerror=alert(1)` was rendered as an `` element with an `onerror` attribute. The JSX renderer used for MDX did not filter string tag names at all. For example: ```astro --- const Tag = Astro.url.searchParams.get('as') ?? 'div'; --- hello ``` rendered `?as=img/src/onerror=alert(1)` as live HTML. ## Impact Reflected or stored cross-site scripting, but only in applications that use untrusted input (such as a request parameter or an uncontrolled CMS field) as all or part of an element name. Astro itself never derives element names from request data. Applications that let content choose an element should map that input to a fixed set of known tags. Letting untrusted input choose an element name is unsafe even with a correct filter, because it can still select elements such as `script` or `iframe`. ## Affected versions `astro` <= 7.4.4. ## Patches Fixed in `astro` 7.4.5. String tag names in `.astro` dynamic tags, JSX, and MDX now render only the leading valid element name, so characters such as `/` or `=` can no longer change the generated markup. Strings that do not start with a valid element name now throw an error. ## Workarounds Upgrade to `astro` 7.4.5 or later. Before upgrading, do not use untrusted input as an element name, or map it to a fixed set of known tags. ## Credits Reported by @uttej-badwane.

advisories.summary: Astro: Image endpoint in @astrojs/node can read files from a case-variant sibling of the output directory on case-sensitive filesystems
advisories.description:
## Summary

The `/_image` endpoint used by the `@astrojs/node` adapter checks that a requested local image is inside the build output directory before reading it from disk. That check compared paths case-insensitively. On case-sensitive filesystems (such as Linux), a directory whose path differs from the output directory only by letter case is a different directory, but it passed the check.

For example, with the client output directory at `/srv/app/dist/client/`, a request such as:

```text
/_image?href=/../../DIST/client/secret.png&w=32&f=png
```

resolved to `/srv/app/DIST/client/secret.png` and was served, even though that file is outside the output directory.

## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can read image files from outside the output directory, but only when all of the following are true:

- The site uses on-demand rendering with the `@astrojs/node` adapter.
- The server runs on a case-sensitive filesystem.
- A directory exists whose path matches the output directory except for letter case (for example `DIST/client` next to `dist/client`). Such a layout is unusual, and the attacker cannot create it.

Only files the image service accepts can be read. Raster images are returned after resizing; SVG files are returned unchanged. Other file types fail during processing. Plain path traversal outside the output directory (for example `/../../secret.png`) was already rejected and is not affected.

## Affected versions

`astro` >= 5.14.3, <= 7.4.6, when used with `@astrojs/node` (all versions up to 11.1.11). The vulnerable image endpoint is provided by `astro` and used by the `@astrojs/node` adapter.

## Patches

Fixed in `astro` 7.4.7. The path check now compares paths exactly, and only ignores letter case for Windows drive-letter paths. The fix ships in `astro`, so upgrading `@astrojs/node` alone is not enough.

## Workarounds

Upgrade to `astro` 7.4.7 or later. Before upgrading, make sure no directory next to the build output directory has a path that differs from it only by letter case.

## Credits

Reported by @zachariah-mithani.

advisories.summary: Nuxt dev server serves files from a parent directory with a stray lockfile or workspace file
advisories.description:
### Summary

Nuxt can pick a parent directory that does not declare a workspace as its default `workspaceDir`: the farthest directory with a lockfile when the project is not inside a git repository, or the farthest directory with a `pnpm-workspace.yaml` or `deno.json` file, even one that only holds settings. The Vite dev server allows `/_nuxt/@fs/` requests for any file under `workspaceDir`. A stray lockfile or settings file in a parent directory, such as the home directory, therefore lets anyone who can reach the dev server read files in that directory and everything below it.

### Impact

This affects the development server only; production builds are not affected. All of the following have to hold:

- A parent directory contains either:
  - a lockfile (`package-lock.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `yarn.lock`, `bun.lock` and similar), while the project is not inside a git repository and has no workspace file (`pnpm-workspace.yaml`, `turbo.json`, `lerna.json` and similar) above it. Running `npm install` once in the home directory is enough to create one there.
  - a `pnpm-workspace.yaml` without a `packages` list (for example one that only holds pnpm settings such as `onlyBuiltDependencies`), or a `deno.json` or `deno.jsonc` without a `workspace` field. This applies even if the project is inside a git repository.
- The dev server is reachable from the network (`nuxt dev --host`, `nuxt dev --tunnel`, a published container port, or a proxy onto the dev port). The default localhost bind limits this to local processes, which can usually read the same files directly.

For example, with `~/package-lock.json` and a project at `~/projects/app` that has no `.git` directory, `nuxt dev --host` serves `GET /_nuxt/@fs/<home>/.ssh/id_ed25519` with status 200. Any file in the home directory that is not covered by Vite's `server.fs.deny` list can be read this way, including SSH keys, cloud credentials and the Nuxt DevTools auth token in `~/.nuxt/devtools/dev-auth-token.txt`.

No browser is involved: a plain HTTP client is enough. A web page on another origin cannot read the response, and DNS rebinding is rejected by Vite's host check.

Projects whose parent directories contain none of these files are not affected, nor are projects inside a git repository whose only lockfile is their own. Nuxt 3.5.0 and later are affected.

### Patches

Fixed in `@nuxt/schema` 4.6.4, which `nuxt` 4.6.4 depends on. A parent directory now only becomes the default `workspaceDir` if it declares a w

advisories.summary: rails-html-sanitizer: Possible XSS via shared scrubber state in concurrent calls
advisories.description:
## Summary

`Rails::HTML::SafeListSanitizer` (both the HTML4 and HTML5 variants) shares one `Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber` across every `sanitize` call on the same instance, assigning its `tags` and `attributes` on each call without synchronization. Two concurrent `sanitize` calls with different `tags:` or `attributes:` options can interleave, so one call is scrubbed with the other call's allowlist.

- Versions affected: `< 1.7.2`
- Not affected: none
- Fixed versions: `1.7.2`

## Impact

Action View memoizes a single `SafeListSanitizer` per helper module and uses it for every `sanitize` call in the process, so in a multi-threaded server (for example Puma) all requests share the same `PermitScrubber`. If any code path calls `sanitize` with a more permissive allowlist, an attacker who can trigger that path concurrently with another request can cause the other request to be sanitized with the permissive allowlist. If the permissive allowlist admits `script` or an event-handler attribute, the strict call emits it unchanged, which is a cross-site scripting vector when the strict output is stored or rendered to other users.

Applications are affected only if they run more than one thread per process and some `sanitize` call passes `tags:` or `attributes:` options that differ from another call's, including a call that passes no options and so uses the defaults. Applications that use a single configuration everywhere, pass their own `scrubber:`, or run single-threaded are not affected.

## Workarounds

Use the same allowlist for every `sanitize` call, or pass a `scrubber:` built per call (`Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber.new` with `tags=` and `attributes=` set) instead of `tags:` and `attributes:` options.

## Credit

Reported by hiumee via HackerOne.

advisories.summary: envd: Host file disclosure through requirements path traversal and TOCTOU
advisories.description:
### Summary

envd’s `install.python_packages(requirements=...)` could read files outside the build context on the host. Content interpreted as dependency entries could appear in build logs and build-step metadata.

Commit f576c92, released in v1.3.5, added path containment validation but left a time-of-check/time-of-use (TOCTOU) race between symlink resolution and opening the requirements file. Commit 9d575b3 addresses this race by opening requirements files through a directory-rooted filesystem handle.

### Details

envd reads requirements files on the host to determine whether their contents can be embedded directly into a pip installation build step.

The vulnerable host-side requirements read was introduced in v0.3.38. Version v1.3.5 added containment checks for static path escapes but remained vulnerable to a TOCTOU race. The complete fix is included in v1.3.6.

Before f576c92, this host read lacked a build-context containment check. That commit added frontend path validation and a compile-time check using filepath.EvalSymlinks followed by a containment comparison.

However, symlink resolution returns a pathname rather than a pinned filesystem object. The subsequent os.Open independently resolves that pathname. Concurrent filesystem changes could therefore invalidate the containment check before the file was opened.

The complete fix uses os.OpenRoot and Root.Open to enforce containment during filesystem traversal.

Resources:
- first commit: be783264fdd79ad7262cea0485b7d449ca514f80
- Initial containment fix: f576c92
- TOCTOU fix: 9d575b3

### Proof of concept

The security-relevant condition is a requirements-file pathname whose filesystem resolution changes between validation and opening. The containment check describes the filesystem at validation time, while the later pathname-based open may access a different object.

The fix includes a deterministic regression test for the underlying object-pinning guarantee. It opens a context directory handle, moves that directory, and creates a replacement directory at the original pathname containing different requirements. The rooted reader continues reading the original context; a pathname-based reader reads the replacement.

This regression test demonstrates the distinction between rooted and pathname-based reads. It is not an end-to-end demonstration of host file disclosure.

advisories.summary: rails-html-sanitizer: Possible regular expression denial of service with certain configurations
advisories.description:
## Summary

`Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber` restricts the `href` and `xlink:href` attributes of SVG reference elements to local references. That check matched the attribute value against `/^\s*[^#\s].*/m`. In Ruby `^` anchors to every line start and `\s` matches newlines, so an all-whitespace value made the engine rescan the value from each of its line starts, taking time quadratic in its length.

- Versions affected: `>= 1.0.3, < 1.7.2`
- Not affected: `< 1.0.3`
- Fixed versions: `1.7.2`

Only Ruby 3.1 and earlier are affected. Ruby 3.2 added linear-time regexp matching, which makes the pattern linear.

## Impact

An attacker who supplies HTML to be sanitized can consume CPU out of proportion to the input size, by sending an SVG reference element whose `href` or `xlink:href` is a long run of whitespace.

Applications are affected only when the allowed tags are overridden to include an SVG reference element such as `use`, along with `href` or `xlink:href` in the allowed attributes. The default allowed tags include no SVG elements, so the default configuration is not affected. Applications that use Loofah directly are exposed through its own copy of the check, fixed in Loofah 2.25.3.

## Workarounds

Run Ruby 3.2 or later, which matches the pattern in linear time, or remove the SVG reference elements from the overridden allowed tags.

## Credit

Reported by scyoon through the Rails HackerOne program.

advisories.summary: OpenTelemetry Python API: Denial of service through quadratic-time traceparent parsing
advisories.description:
## Summary

`TraceContextTextMapPropagator.extract()` in `opentelemetry-api` is vulnerable to regular expression denial of service (ReDoS) when processing a specially crafted `traceparent` value.

A malformed value containing a trace-context prefix followed by a long whitespace sequence and an embedded newline triggers quadratic-time regex backtracking. Applications that extract trace context from untrusted carriers accepting such strings can experience excessive CPU consumption and request-processing delays.

When extraction runs on an asynchronous server’s event-loop thread, a single malicious message can delay unrelated requests handled by that event loop.

## Exposure conditions

Exploitation requires attacker-controlled input to reach the affected propagator through a carrier that preserves embedded newlines and permits a sufficiently large value.

Conforming HTTP header values cannot contain embedded newlines. However, OpenTelemetry carriers are not restricted to HTTP headers. JSON strings can contain escaped newlines that become newline characters after decoding.

MCP request metadata is one relevant integration path: applications may extract trace context from JSON `params._meta`. Exposure depends on the MCP SDK or instrumentation version, whether extraction invokes the W3C Trace Context propagator, and applicable message-size limits. HTTP header validation does not constrain a `traceparent` string carried inside a JSON body.

Authentication requirements depend on the application exposing the carrier.

## Impact

The demonstrated impact is denial of service through excessive CPU consumption and blocked request processing. Repeated malicious messages may sustain service degradation.

This finding does not demonstrate data disclosure, data modification, or code execution.

## Remediation

Upgrade `opentelemetry-api` to `1.45.2` or a later release containing the fix.

Version `1.45.2` rejects `traceparent` values longer than 512 characters before regex matching and removes the overlapping suffix and trailing-whitespace expressions.

Where upgrading is temporarily unavailable, reject oversized values and embedded CR/LF characters before passing untrusted trace-context values to the affected propagator.

advisories.summary: Soup Sieve: Exponential ReDoS in selector compilation via \9-run in CSS_ESCAPES/IDENTIFIER
advisories.description:
### Summary
The IDENTIFIER/CSS_ESCAPES regex (css_parser.py:119-124) exhibits exponential backtracking on a run of ambiguous digit-escapes (`\9`) in an attribute-name or tag position of an otherwise well-formed selector. It fires at compile time (before the SELECTOR_LIMIT guard) via the public `soupsieve.compile()` and BeautifulSoup `.select()`.

### PoC (verified on soupsieve 2.9.2)

    import soupsieve as sv
    sv.compile('[a' + '\\9'*26 + '=x]')   # ~57 bytes -> ~10s; ~16x time per +4 chars

### Novelty
Distinct from the patched GHSA-836r-... (VALUE regex) and GHSA-2wc2-... (comma-list) advisories, which are fixed in 2.9.2; this is a different regex/vector.

### Reachability
CSS selectors are usually developer-controlled, so exposure requires an application that compiles UNTRUSTED selector strings (web-scraping-as-a-service, no-code/query builders, user-defined extraction rules). Where selectors are user-supplied, a ~60-byte string hangs the worker.

### Note
This issue was fixed in version 3.0.0, which has been yanked from the PyPI registry. Use versions 3.0.2 and above to upgrade.

advisories.summary: Soup Sieve: Uncontrolled recursion in CSS parser lets nested pseudo-class selectors exhaust the Python call stack
advisories.description:
## Summary

The Soup Sieve CSS selector parser recurses once per level of nested pseudo-class selector (`:is()`, `:not()`, `:where()`, `:has()`) without any limit on nesting depth. An unauthenticated attacker who can supply a CSS selector string to `soupsieve.compile()`, `soupsieve.select()`, or Beautiful Soup's `soup.select()` / `soup.select_one()` can force the parser to exceed Python's recursion limit with a small crafted input (about 1.6 KB, roughly 330 nesting levels), raising an uncontrolled `RecursionError`. Because this exception is not part of the parser's documented error contract, applications that catch only `ValueError` or `SelectorSyntaxError` see an unexpected failure of the request or task that parsed the selector.

## Root Cause

The parser dispatches each opening pseudo-class token to `parse_pseudo_open`, which calls back into `parse_selectors` to parse the pseudo-class body. Every nesting level therefore adds Python stack frames, and no counter, depth guard, or `RecursionError` handler bounds this descent. The token-count guard `SELECTOR_LIMIT = 8192` (added for the earlier comma-separated-list memory issue) counts parsed tokens, not recursion depth; at the failing nesting depth the token count is only about 330, roughly four percent of that limit, so the guard never fires. The security invariant that untrusted selector input must not be able to exhaust interpreter resources is not enforced for nesting depth.

```text
soupsieve/css_parser.py
  CSSParser.parse_pseudo_open (line 985): sel.selectors.append(self.parse_selectors(iselector, index, flags))
  CSSParser.parse_selectors  (line 1137): recursive target; dispatches pseudo-class tokens back into parse_pseudo_class -> parse_pseudo_open
  CSSParser.increment_count  (lines 707-712): SELECTOR_LIMIT token guard; increments once per nesting level, cannot bound depth
```

## Impact

Any application that compiles or evaluates untrusted CSS selectors through Soup Sieve (directly or via Beautiful Soup) is affected. No authentication, privilege, or user interaction is required; the failure occurs during selector parsing, before any document is matched. A single crafted selector of about 1.6 KB reliably raises `RecursionError`. The demonstrated capability is a transient denial of the individual request, task, or invocation that parsed the malicious selector: the exception propagates uncaught unless the caller handles `RecursionError` (or a broad `except Exception`). advisories.summary: Zebra's Block Validator Undercounts Coinbase and P2SH Sigops
advisories.description:
Zebra's block validator undercounts transparent signature operations against the 20000-sigop block limit (`MAX_BLOCK_SIGOPS`), allowing it to accept blocks that `zcashd` rejects with `bad-blk-sigops`. A miner who produces such a block can split the network: Zebra nodes follow the offending chain while `zcashd` nodes do not.

Two distinct undercounts:

#### A: Coinbase Hidden Legacy Sigops

`zcashd`'s `GetLegacySigOpCount()` includes the coinbase input's `scriptSig`. Zebra's `Sigops` impl skipped the coinbase input entirely, so up to ~98 sigops (the 100-byte coinbase script length cap, less the height prefix) could be hidden inside the coinbase `scriptSig` without being charged against the block limit.

#### B: Aggregate P2SH Sigops.

`zcashd`'s `GetP2SHSigOpCount()` parses each P2SH input's redeem script with `accurate=true` and sums those sigops into the block-wide total via `ConnectBlock`. The check is per-block, not per-transaction, and the limit applies regardless of who mines the offending block — a miner just needs to include enough P2SH-spending transactions whose redeem scripts together exceed 20000 sigops. Zebra computed P2SH sigops only on the mempool-acceptance path (used for ZIP-317 weighting) and never accumulated them during block validation. A block whose aggregate redeem-script sigops exceed 20000 (e.g. 1334 P2SH spends × 15 sigops = 20010) would be accepted by Zebra and rejected by `zcashd`.

### Patches

Fixed in this release:  https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v4.4.0.

### Workarounds

None. Operators relying on Zebra for consensus should upgrade.

### Resources

- `MAX_BLOCK_SIGOPS` constant inherited from Bitcoin via the Zcash protocol spec's §7.6 catch-all "Other rules inherited from Bitcoin", tracked for explicit documentation in [zcash/zips#568](https://github.com/zcash/zips/issues/568).
- `zcashd` `GetLegacySigOpCount`: <https://github.com/zcash/zcash/blob/v6.11.0/src/main.cpp#L826-L836>
- `zcashd` `GetP2SHSigOpCount`: <https://github.com/zcash/zcash/blob/v6.11.0/src/main.cpp#L840-L852>
- `zcashd` `ConnectBlock` aggregates per-tx sigops and compares against `MAX_BLOCK_SIGOPS`.

advisories.summary: Zebra's Transparent SIGHASH_SINGLE Handling Diverges from zcashd for Corresponding Outputs

# `Zebra` Transparent `SIGHASH_SINGLE` Corresponding-Output Handling Diverges From `zcashd`

### Summary
For V5+ transparent spends, `Zebra` and `zcashd` disagree on the same consensus rule: `SIGHASH_SINGLE` must fail when the input index has no corresponding output. `zcashd` treats this as consensus-invalid under ZIP-244, while `Zebra`'s transparent verification path computes a digest for the missing-output case instead of failing.

The result is a direct block-validity split. A malformed V5 transparent transaction can be accepted by `Zebra`, retained in `Zebra`'s mempool, selected into `Zebra` `getblocktemplate`, mined into a block, and then rejected by `zcashd`.

### Details
Validated code revisions used during analysis:

- `zcashd`: `2c63e9aa08cb170b0feb374161bea94720c3e1f5`
- `Zebra`: `a905fa19e3a91c7b4ead331e2709e6dec5db12cb`

Scope note:

- earlier triage material grouped pre-V5 and V5 behavior together;
- re-execution on the pinned revisions did not reproduce the claimed pre-V5 / V4 reject-side behavior;
- this advisory therefore covers the V5+ / ZIP-244 variant only.

`zcashd` side:

- Transparent scripts in blocks are checked through `TransactionSignatureChecker::CheckSig()` and `SignatureHash()`: [`zcash/src/script/interpreter.cpp`](https://github.com/zcash/zcash/blob/2c63e9aa08cb170b0feb374161bea94720c3e1f5/src/script/interpreter.cpp#L1386-L1407).
- In the ZIP-244 branch, `SignatureHash()` explicitly throws when `SIGHASH_SINGLE` or `SIGHASH_SINGLE|ANYONECANPAY` is used with `nIn >= txTo.vout.size()`: [`zcash/src/script/interpreter.cpp`](https://github.com/zcash/zcash/blob/2c63e9aa08cb170b0feb374161bea94720c3e1f5/src/script/interpreter.cpp#L1221-L1259).
- `CheckSig()` catches that exception and returns `false`, causing the transparent script to fail.

`Zebra` side:

- V5 transparent inputs route into the same FFI-based transparent script verifier used for block validation: [`zebra/zebra-consensus/src/transaction.rs`](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/blob/a905fa19e3a91c7b4ead331e2709e6dec5db12cb/zebra-consensus/src/transaction.rs#L989-L1098).
- `Zebra` converts the decoded hash type and asks its Rust sighash engine for a digest without adding the corresponding-output pre-check that `zcashd` enforces first: [`zebra/zebra-script/src/lib.rs`](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/blob/a905fa19e3a91c7b4ead331e2709e6dec5db12cb/zebra-script/src/lib.rs#L160-L175), [`zebra/zebra-chain/src/primitives/zcash_primitives.rs`](https://github.com/Zca

advisories.summary: zebrad has full node denial of service via non-ASCII LongPollId in getblocktemplate
advisories.description:
### Am I affected

You are affected if:

1. You run `zebrad` up to and including `v4.4.1`.
2. Your `zebrad.toml` sets `rpc.listen_addr` to a TCP address (RPC server is enabled).
3. An attacker can authenticate to the RPC endpoint. With the default `enable_cookie_auth = true`, this requires the attacker to read the `.cookie` file. With `enable_cookie_auth = false`, any network client reaching the RPC port can trigger it.

### Summary

The `getblocktemplate` RPC handler panics when parsing a `LongPollId` parameter that contains non-ASCII (multi-byte UTF-8) characters. The handler performs byte-index string slicing on the user-supplied string, which panics in Rust when a byte index falls within a multi-byte character boundary. Because Zebra's release profile sets `panic = "abort"`, the panic terminates the entire node process.

### Details

The `getblocktemplate` handler receives a user-supplied `LongPollId` string and slices it at fixed byte offsets to extract the encoded tip hash and tip height. When the string contains multi-byte UTF-8 characters, a byte-index slice can land in the middle of a character, causing Rust's `str` indexing to panic with "byte index is not a char boundary."

Under the `panic = "abort"` release profile, this panic terminates the entire `zebrad` process rather than just the RPC task.

### Patches

zebra-rpc 8.0.0 and zebrad 4.5.0.

Replace byte-index string slicing with character-aware parsing or validate that the `LongPollId` string contains only ASCII characters before slicing.

### Workarounds

- Disable the RPC server by removing `rpc.listen_addr` from `zebrad.toml`.
- Ensure `enable_cookie_auth = true` (the default) and restrict filesystem access to the `.cookie` file.
- Place a reverse proxy in front of the RPC port that validates `LongPollId` parameters are ASCII-only before forwarding.

### Impact

A single authenticated RPC request terminates the `zebrad` process. Same impact profile as GHSA-c8w6-x74f-vmg3: repeatable on restart, affects mining pools and infrastructure that forward `getblocktemplate` calls.

### Credit

Reported by `@sangsoo-osec` via a private GitHub Security Advisory submission.

advisories.summary: zebrad has mempool transaction admission denial via single-peer inbound queue saturation
advisories.description:
### Am I affected

You are affected if:

1. You run `zebrad` up to and including `v4.4.1`.
2. Your node accepts inbound P2P connections (`network.listen_addr` is set, which is the default).
3. Your node's mempool is active (node is synced near the chain tip).

All default configurations are affected.

### Summary

A single unauthenticated P2P peer can monopolize all 25 inbound mempool download/verification slots (`MAX_INBOUND_CONCURRENCY`) by advertising fake transaction IDs. While the slots are occupied, all other inbound transactions from honest peers and local RPC `sendrawtransaction` calls are rejected with `MempoolError::FullQueue`. The attacker peer is never scored for misbehavior and is not disconnected, allowing sustained denial of mempool admission.

### Details

The mempool download/verification pipeline at `zebrad/src/components/mempool/downloads.rs` uses a single bounded pool of 25 concurrent tasks. Three architectural gaps combine to produce the vulnerability:

1. No per-peer accounting: the 25 slots are shared across all peers with no cap on how many a single peer can hold.
2. No overload signaling: when `FullQueue` is returned, the inbound service at `zebrad/src/components/inbound.rs` maps it to `Response::Nil`, hiding the overload from the peer connection layer. The existing `handle_inbound_overload` disconnection logic never fires.
3. No misbehavior attribution: peer identity is not carried through the `Gossip` type into the download pipeline, so verification failures cannot be attributed to the originating peer.

The attacker sends `inv` messages advertising fake transaction IDs. Zebra queues download tasks for each ID. The attacker stays silent; each slot is held until the `TRANSACTION_DOWNLOAD_TIMEOUT` (20 seconds) fires. The attacker periodically sends fresh `inv` waves to re-fill slots as they expire.

Two additional slot-holding techniques have been independently demonstrated: invalid-prevout transactions that park in `AwaitOutput` for 60 seconds, and expensive shielded proof verification with auth-variant cache bypass. All three techniques are addressed by the same per-peer accounting fix.

### Patches

zebrad 4.5.0

The fix adds per-peer queue accounting to the mempool download pipeline. A single peer is limited to a fraction of `MAX_INBOUND_CONCURRENCY` (e.g., 5 slots out of 25). `FullQueue` is surfaced as an overload signal to the peer connection layer. Peer identity is plumbed through the `Gossip` type for misbehavior attributio

advisories.summary: Zebra has Permanent Block Discovery Halt via Gossip Queue Saturation and Syncer Poisoning
advisories.description:
## Summary

A composite denial-of-service vulnerability in Zebra's block discovery pipeline allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to permanently halt all new block discovery on a targeted node. The attack exploits three independent weaknesses in the gossip, syncer, and download subsystems — all exercisable from a single TCP connection — to create a monotonically growing block deficit that never self-heals.

## Severity

**Critical** — This is a Denial of Service vulnerability that requires no authentication, no special privileges, and only a single peer connection. The halt is permanent: the node will never recover without operator intervention.

## Affected Versions

All Zebra versions prior to 4.4.0.

## Description

Zebra discovers new blocks through two complementary paths: a gossip path (peers announce blocks via `inv` messages, triggering individual block downloads) and a syncer path (Zebra periodically queries peers with `FindBlocks`/`FindHeaders` to discover chains of missing blocks). Both paths must function for normal operation.

The gossip path was vulnerable because there was no per-connection rate limit on `inv` messages. A single connection could send enough sequential `inv` messages with fake block hashes to fill the entire gossip download queue in under a millisecond. The `FullQueue` return value was silently ignored, so legitimate block announcements from honest peers were dropped with no warning.

The syncer backup path could be degraded by responding with empty `inv` to `FindBlocks` requests and with `NotFound` to block download requests. Both are valid protocol responses that carried zero misbehavior penalty. The attacker's connection was never banned and never disconnected, allowing the degradation to persist indefinitely.

Combining these two vectors, an attacker could suppress both block discovery paths simultaneously from a single connection, causing the node to fall permanently behind the chain tip.

## Impact

**Denial of Service**

* **Attack Vector:** Network, unauthenticated. Requires only a single TCP peer connection.
* **Effect:** Permanent halt of block discovery. The targeted node falls behind the chain tip and never recovers without operator intervention.
* **Scope:** Any Zebra node reachable by the attacker over the peer-to-peer network.

## Fixed Versions

This issue is fixed in Zebra 4.4.0.

The fix drops connections that send empty responses to `FindBlocks` and `FindHeaders` messages, preventing attackers from degr

advisories.description:
### Am I affected

You are affected if:

1. You run `zebrad` up to and including `v4.4.1`.
2. Your node participates in a network where chain forks occur (mainnet, testnet, or any network with multiple miners).

All default configurations are affected. The corruption persists across restarts because it is written to RocksDB.

### Summary

When `pop_tip` removes the tip block during a chain fork, stale Sapling and Orchard note commitment subtree root data is retained in the in-memory non-finalized state. When the chain subsequently finalizes, this stale data is written to the persistent RocksDB state. The corrupted subtree root history affects `z_getsubtreesbyindex` (used by lightwalletd for wallet synchronization) and could affect future chain verification that depends on correct subtree roots.

### Details

The non-finalized state provides two methods for removing blocks: `pop_root` (removes the oldest block during finalization) and `pop_tip` (removes the newest block during a fork revert). `pop_root` correctly cleans up note commitment subtree contributions. `pop_tip` does not: it removes the block but retains the block's subtree root contributions in the in-memory state.

When a chain fork occurs and `pop_tip` reverts the old tip, the winning fork's chain is extended. When that chain is later finalized, the stale subtree data from the reverted blocks is included in the RocksDB write batch and persisted to disk.

The `pop_root`/`pop_tip` asymmetry is specific to subtree root handling. Other state managed by `pop_tip` (nullifiers, UTXOs, anchors, block hashes) uses different cleanup patterns that are not affected.

### Patches

zebra-state 7.0.0 and zebrad 4.5.0.

The fix adds subtree root cleanup to `pop_tip` matching the pattern already used by `pop_root`.

### Workarounds

There is no configuration-level workaround. Chain forks are natural events on any Proof-of-Work network. Operators can mitigate the downstream impact by periodically verifying subtree root consistency using `z_getsubtreesbyindex` against a known-good reference.

### Impact

Persistent corruption of Sapling and Orchard subtree root history in the RocksDB state database. The corruption survives node restarts. Downstream consumers that rely on `z_getsubtreesbyindex` for wallet synchronization (primarily `lightwalletd` and light wallets) receive incorrect subtree roots. advisories.summary: zebrad has unbounded memory leak in mempool download pipeline via timeout path cancel_handles retention
advisories.description:
### Am I affected

You are affected if:

1. You run `zebrad` up to and including `v4.4.1`.
2. Your node accepts inbound P2P connections (`network.listen_addr` is set, which is the default).
3. Your node's mempool is active (node is synced near the chain tip).

All default configurations are affected.

### Summary

The mempool download pipeline's `cancel_handles` map retains entries for transactions whose verification times out at the outer `RATE_LIMIT_DELAY` (73-second) boundary. The `tokio::time::error::Elapsed` error carries no payload, so the transaction ID is unrecoverable and the corresponding `cancel_handles` entry (including the full `Gossip::Tx(UnminedTx)`, up to ~2 MB) is never removed. Entries accumulate monotonically with no upper bound or garbage collection, leading to eventual out-of-memory process termination.

### Details

`Downloads::poll_next()` at `zebrad/src/components/mempool/downloads.rs:215-228` handles three terminal states for a verification task:

- `Ok(Ok(...))`: success. Calls `cancel_handles.remove(&tx.transaction.id)`. Correct.
- `Ok(Err(...))`: verification error. Calls `cancel_handles.remove(&hash)`. Correct.
- `Err(elapsed)`: outer timeout. Returns `Err(elapsed)` without removing anything. **Bug.**

`tokio::time::error::Elapsed` has no payload, so the timed-out transaction's `UnminedTxId` is unrecoverable from the error. The consumer at `zebrad/src/components/mempool.rs:663-672` explicitly acknowledges this gap with a TODO comment.

The only cleanup paths for `cancel_handles` are `cancel(mined_ids)` (removes entries matching mined transaction IDs; attacker transactions are never mined) and `cancel_all()` (clears everything on shutdown or chain reset). No periodic GC, no time-based eviction, and no count cap exists.

For direct `tx` pushes (`Gossip::Tx`), the retained entry holds the full deserialized transaction, which can be up to ~9 MB in memory for a transaction near the transparent-output extreme. Per-connection leak rate at worst case: ~685 KB/s (~2.4 GB/hour).

### Patches

The fix preserves the `UnminedTxId` through the timeout error path: wrap the timeout future so the spawned task's outer error carries the txid (e.g., `Err((txid, elapsed))`). In `Downloads::poll_next()`, on the timeout arm, call `cancel_handles.remove(&txid)`.

### Workarounds

There is no configuration-level workaround. Restarting the node clears the accumulated entries. Operators running in memory-constrained environments (containers with cgroup l

advisories.summary: Zebra Address Book Aborted by IPv4-Mapped Mempool Misbehavior Update
advisories.description:
### Am I affected

You are affected if:

1. You run `zebrad` up to and including `v4.4.1`.
2. Your node listens on the default `[::]` address on a Linux host (the standard deployment configuration — `net.ipv6.bindv6only=0` is the default on all common Linux distributions).
3. Your node is synced near the chain tip (the expected production state for any node participating in the network).

### Summary

An address normalization mismatch between the handshake path and the mempool misbehavior path causes a deterministic assertion panic when a peer connects via IPv4 to a dual-stack IPv6 listener and then triggers a mempool misbehavior penalty.

The handshake path canonicalizes IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses to plain IPv4 when storing the peer in the address book via `MetaAddr::new_connected`. The mempool misbehavior path forwards the raw transient socket address (IPv4-mapped IPv6 form) when sending `MetaAddrChange::UpdateMisbehavior` to the address book. The address book looks up the canonical IPv4 entry but then asserts that the previous entry's address matches the change's address. The mismatch between the canonical IPv4 address and the raw IPv4-mapped IPv6 address triggers the assertion, and `panic = "abort"` terminates the process.

### Details

On Linux with `net.ipv6.bindv6only=0`, an IPv4 connection accepted by a `[::]` listener is represented internally as an IPv4-mapped IPv6 socket address (e.g., `::ffff:127.0.0.1:8233`). Zebra's `canonical_peer_addr` helper converts these to plain IPv4 (e.g., `127.0.0.1:8233`).

The handshake path uses `MetaAddr::new_connected`, which canonicalizes the address before storing in the address book. However, inbound inventory registration uses `connected_addr.get_transient_addr()`, preserving the raw IPv4-mapped form. When the mempool later downloads an invalid transaction from this peer and generates a misbehavior penalty, the raw transient address is forwarded through the misbehavior channel to `MetaAddrChange::UpdateMisbehavior`, which does not canonicalize.

After the 30-second misbehavior batch flush, `AddressBook::update` retrieves the canonical IPv4 entry but `MetaAddrChange::apply_to_meta_addr` asserts that `previous.addr == self.addr()`, which fails because one is IPv4 and the other is IPv4-mapped IPv6.

The attacker needs only to complete a P2P handshake over IPv4 to a dual-stack listener and advertise an invalid mempool transaction (such as a coinbase transaction). The assertion fires after the 30-second misbehavio

advisories.summary: Rucio: Unauthenticated administrator impersonation through SSH challenge tokens
advisories.description:
## Summary

SSH challenge tokens are mistakenly accepted as valid credentials during the authentication token validation process.

While an SSH challenge token is intended as a short-lived nonce for use in a subsequent SSH key exchange, the function to validate authentication tokens does not differentiate between these and actual authentication tokens. Because challenge tokens are generated based on an account name provided via headers without requiring prior authentication, an unauthenticated attacker can request a valid "challenge" token for any account (including administrative ones) and use it to authenticate against other API endpoints.

## Proof of Concept

The vulnerability exists because SSH challenge tokens are stored in the same database table as regular authentication tokens and `validate_auth_token` in `lib/rucio/core/authentication.py` accepts these "challenge" tokens. An attacker can obtain a challenge token for an account such as “root” via the REST API and then present it as a valid authentication bearer token:

1. Request a challenge token for an arbitrary account (e.g., "root"):
   `curl -i -H "X-Rucio-Account: root" https://rucio/auth/ssh_challenge_token`
2. The server returns a `200 OK` with the header `X-Rucio-SSH-Challenge-Token`.
3. The attacker can then use this specific token within the ten-second challenge lifetime as an authentication credential in subsequent requests to the Rucio API:
  `curl -H "X-Rucio-Auth-Token: $CHALLENGE_TOKEN"  https://rucio/accounts/whoami`

advisories.summary: Soup Sieve: Polynomial-time denial of service in the descendant combinator
advisories.description:
## Summary

Matching a selector that uses the descendant combinator (`a b`) takes time that grows polynomially with how deeply the document is nested, and each extra descendant combinator in the selector raises the degree by one. A selector with `k` descendant combinators takes `O(n^(k+1))` time on a chain of `n` nested elements.

An attacker who controls the HTML or XML that an application passes to Soup Sieve (directly, or through Beautiful Soup's `select()`, `select_one()`, `css.select()`, etc.) can send a very small, deeply nested document that keeps a CPU busy for seconds to minutes against an ordinary selector such as `section div div`.

## Details

To match `a b`, Soup Sieve checks each element against `b` and then walks up through its ancestors looking for one that matches `a`. When the selector has more descendant combinators, the rest of the selector is tried again from each ancestor on that walk, and so on for every combinator. Nothing was reused between walks, so the same ancestors were matched against the same part of the selector over and over.

The worst case is when the leftmost part of the selector never matches, as in `section div div` against a document of nested `<div>` with no `<section>`: every walk goes all the way to the root and no search can stop early.

### Timings

Example timings with `html.parser` on Soup Sieve 3.0.4 and 4.0, using a document of nested `<div>` (5 bytes each) and no matches:

| Nesting depth | Input size | Selector | 3.0.4 | 4.0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2,000 | 10 KB | `section div` | 1.6 s | 0.05 s |
| 4,000 | 20 KB | `section div` | 5.1 s | 0.01 s |
| 400 | 2 KB | `section div div` | 6.7 s | < 0.01 s |
| 800 | 4 KB | `section div div` | 53.0 s | < 0.01 s |
| 100 | 0.5 KB | `section div div div` | 2.5 s | < 0.01 s |
| 200 | 1 KB | `section div div div` | 40.9 s | < 0.01 s |

None of these selectors use unusual syntax.

## Proof of concept

```py
import time
import bs4
import soupsieve as sv

soup = bs4.BeautifulSoup('<div>' * 200, 'html.parser')
t = time.process_time()
sv.select('section div div div', soup)
print(time.process_time() - t)
```

On affected versions, doubling the nesting depth multiplies the time by about 2^(k+1), where `k` is the number of descendant combinators: about 4x for `section div`, 8x for `section div div`, and 16x for `section div div div`.

## Impact

Applications are affected if they run selectors with descendant combinators against documents that untrusted users can influ

advisories.description:
## Summary Matching a selector that puts a general-sibling combinator inside `:has()`, such as `div:has(a ~ b)`, against untrusted HTML runs in O(n²) time in the number of sibling elements. A single small document with a few thousand siblings ties the process up for a minute of CPU, so an application that runs a fixed selector of this shape over HTML it doesn't control can be stalled by one request. `:has` is powerful, but much in the same way poor regular expressions can be crafted to cause catastrophic backtracking with greedy capturing, has can be used to create non-ideal scenarios that can cause large portions of the tree to be evaluated for one or many elements if not used thoughtfully. This behavior is not exclusive to Soup Sieve, but browsers make note of these potential performance issues themselves: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Selectors/:has#performance_considerations. With all of that said, there is room for improvements that can in some cases greatly improve performance. ## Details `:has(a ~ b)` asks "does this element contain an `a` that has a later sibling `b`?". When no `b` is present, soupsieve can't short-circuit, and it answers the question with a nested scan: `match_future_child` walks every candidate `a` under the scope, and for each one the general-sibling branch of `match_future_relations` walks all of that `a`'s following siblings looking for `b`. With n siblings that is (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 comparisons, i.e. O(n²). The adjacent-sibling form `div:has(a + b)` stays linear, because its branch checks only the one immediately following sibling per candidate. advisories.summary: Active Storage: Possible arbitrary file write and read in image analysis
advisories.description:
### Impact
A Rails application that processes attachments with ImageMagick may allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on the server and, when attachments are stored with the Disk service, to read arbitrary files readable by the application process. Those files typically include `secret_key_base` and credentials for external systems, which may in turn allow escalation to remote code execution or lateral movement to those systems.

### Details
ImageMagick selects a coder from the content of the file it is given, and some coders act on files named inside the image rather than on the image itself. Active Storage constrained none of ImageMagick's coders, and the ImageMagick analyzer runs when a file is attached, so an attacker who can upload a crafted file may be able to invoke one. Attaching the upload is sufficient; no variant, preview, or `analyze` call is required. One specific attack chain has been reported to us, but we do not assume it is the only one that exists.

The fixed versions ship an ImageMagick security policy and prepend its directory to `MAGICK_CONFIGURE_PATH` through `MiniMagick.cli_env`, so every ImageMagick process that MiniMagick spawns applies it. The policy denies the `MSL` scripting coder, the coders that read or delete files other than the image, fetch remote or local references, or display to a screen, every coder backed by Ghostscript together with the `gs` delegate, and `@filename` indirection. ImageMagick applies every `policy.xml` on its search path, so the shipped policy adds to the host's policy rather than replacing it. The policy applies to every ImageMagick command that MiniMagick runs, not only those of Active Storage. See the `activestorage` CHANGELOG and "ImageMagick Security Policy" in the Active Storage guide.

### Affected applications
An application is affected if it meets all of these requirements:
- Uses ImageMagick for Active Storage image processing. This is `config.active_storage.variant_processor = :mini_magick`, which is the default for applications on `load_defaults 6.1` or earlier.
- Runs ImageMagick under a security policy that does not already deny the coders involved. The policies that Debian and Ubuntu package do not.
- Allows file uploads from untrusted users.

### Mitigation
- Upgrade to a fixed version of `activestorage`.
- An application whose variant processor is `:mini_magick` must use mini_magick `>= 5.1`, which applying the policy requires. With an older mini_magick, such an app

advisories.summary: Action Pack: Possible DoS vulnerability in Action Controller Live streaming
advisories.description:
### Impact
`ActionController::Live::Buffer#close` pushes its end-of-stream marker onto the response's bounded queue while it holds the buffer's monitor. When the client has stopped reading and the queue is full, the push blocks, and `Buffer#abort`, which runs when the client disconnects or a write times out, waits indefinitely for the same monitor. Each such response could permanently hold a web server thread and its `ActionController::Live` thread, possibly resulting in a DoS vulnerability through thread exhaustion.

Applications that stream responses with `ActionController::Live`, including `send_stream`, are affected. Applications that serve large files through Active Storage proxy mode are exposed to unauthenticated clients.

### Releases

advisories.summary: Action Pack: Possible sensitive session information leak in Active Storage proxy mode
advisories.description:
### Impact
When `ActionDispatch::Cookies` reads a signed or encrypted cookie that was written under a rotated secret (`config.action_dispatch.cookies_rotations`) or in the format that a `:hybrid` cookie serializer migrates from, it writes the cookie back to the response in the current format, and that write ignores `request.session_options[:skip]`. `ActiveStorage::DisableSession` relies on that option to keep the session cookie off the public, immutable responses of the Active Storage proxy controllers, but those controllers still load the session, so a request carrying an old-format session cookie could receive the rewritten session cookie in `Set-Cookie` on a cacheable response. A shared cache that stores such a response together with its `Set-Cookie` header could then serve one user's session to later requesters of the same URL, or serve an attacker's session to other users.

Applications are affected when they serve Active Storage files through the proxy controllers, have a cookie rotation or a `:hybrid` serializer migration configured, and run behind a cache that stores `Set-Cookie` on public responses. This is a path around the fix for [CVE-2024-26144](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8h22-8cf7-hq6g).

### Details
In the fixed releases, a response that skips the session leaves an old-format signed or encrypted cookie unchanged, and the next request that does not skip the session upgrades it. An application that skips the session on every request no longer upgrades its signed or encrypted cookies. Cookies that the application sets explicitly are still written. See the Action Pack CHANGELOG.

### Workarounds
Configure caching proxies not to store responses that carry a `Set-Cookie` header, or complete the cookie rotation or serializer migration and remove it from the configuration.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/849a6c30eacbb6ca4722132f43c4333a93188556.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/0e6cf8faa89caf4c64311d35ca2bc88c1458d4e3.patch

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [flashmyname](https://hackerone.com/flashmyname).

advisories.summary: Action View: Possible XSS vulnerability in highlight helper
advisories.description:
### Impact
`ActionView::Helpers::TextHelper#highlight` substitutes each matched phrase into the `:highlighter` string without escaping it and returns the result marked HTML-safe. Because sanitizing leaves quote characters in text unescaped, a match substituted into a quoted attribute value of the highlighter, such as the `<a href="search?q=\1">` form shown in the method's documentation, could end the attribute value and add attributes to the element, possibly leading to XSS. Applications are affected when they pass a `:highlighter` that places a placeholder inside an attribute value and highlight text or phrases that a user controls. The default `<mark>\1</mark>` highlighter and the block form are not affected.

### Details
The fixed releases HTML-escape each group substituted into the `:highlighter` string, so quotes in a match are rendered as `"` and `'`. Only the numbered placeholders `\0` to `\9` are expanded; other `String#sub` replacement escapes, such as `\k<name>`, `\&` and `\\`, are left as written. A match can no longer begin on the `>` that closes a preceding tag. Escaping makes a placeholder safe as element content or inside a quoted attribute value, but not in an unquoted attribute value, a URL, JavaScript or CSS context, or an attribute whose value is HTML. See the Action View CHANGELOG for details.

### Workarounds
Use a `:highlighter` that places the matched phrase only in element content, such as the default `<mark>\1</mark>`.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/06938194b4fd59e1d2c8ab4a781f3c1e2b763425.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/c796f6198837479ada13290eb8fa767b5219a58a.patch

### Credit
This issue was found by the Anthropic OSS Scanner (ANT-2026-THHUJQVO).

advisories.summary: Action View: Possible XSS vulnerability in strip_tags
advisories.description:
### Impact
`strip_tags` in Action View returns its sanitized output marked `html_safe`, but the underlying sanitizer encodes only `&`, `<` and `>`, leaving `"` and `'` unencoded. Because ERB does not escape a string marked `html_safe`, untrusted input passed through `strip_tags` and rendered inside a quoted HTML attribute value could close the attribute and add new attributes, possibly leading to XSS. Applications that render `strip_tags` output from untrusted input inside an HTML attribute, for example in a `title` attribute or a `<meta content>` tag, are affected. Output rendered as element content is not affected.

### Details
`strip_tags` now encodes `"` and `'` in its output, as well as `&`, `<` and `>`, without double-encoding existing entities. Applications that use `strip_tags` output outside HTML, such as in a text template or JSON, now see `"` and `'` where they saw `"` and `'`; `CGI.unescapeHTML` decodes them. See the Action View CHANGELOG.

### Workarounds
Pass `strip_tags` output to an attribute through a tag helper, which escapes attribute values, for example `tag.a(title: strip_tags(user_input))`.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/568b19cb860322885593e308a7f27aceb779e9d7.patch

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [lucasluitjes](https://hackerone.com/lucasluitjes).
